title: How it works · louis-agent
text: How it works One turn, through every layer. You send a message. The API hands it to the engine with the chat so far, and the engine runs the model and its tools until there is an answer. The answer streams back while it is written. Every request to the model on the way passes through the same six layers, listed here outermost first. Every call passes the guards first. the tools kept On the last round, sends the same tool list with tool use switched off. The model answers in text, and the request still matches the ones before it. the usage Writes every request to the ledger, each round as a record of its own. the cut-off calls Marks a tool call that the output limit cut short, so it is never run. the trace Traces the request and its answer with OpenTelemetry. the replay Answers from a recorded run when one is kept, so a replay costs nothing. A turn, step by step The pipeline The web The web, with the backend. A site is C# running in the browser. Its host draws each page first, so a search engine can read it. The agent itself runs behind the API, one session per chat. LouisAgent.Web What every site is built on. It is Blazor WebAssembly, so the site is C# running in the browser. the site's host Draws each page as HTML a search engine can read. Then the app takes over in the browser. LouisAgent.Api Holds the sessions, and streams each turn back as server-sent events while it is written. Every site on the framework's web Every message on the wire Identities Who an agent is. An identity is an agent's voice, its rules and its skills, written as markdown you can read and change. It names the packs it uses. These are the identities in the repo today. LouisAgent.Identities.Coding The coding agent, in Rider and the terminal. LouisAgent.Identities.Triage A team that triages a service's errors. LouisAgent.Identities.Guide The guide on louis-agent.dev, who answers visitors and shows them round. LouisAgent.Identities.Framework The framework's Orbi, who answers developers on this site from the docs. LouisAgent.Identities.Showroom The agents of the showroom's three made-up businesses. Build an identity Packs What an agent can do. A pack is a set of tools in a project of its own. It references no other pack, so an MCP server can serve it just as it is. These are the packs in the repo today. LouisAgent.Packs.Files The workspace's files. Read, write, search, and PDF, Word and Excel as text. LouisAgent.Packs.Git Git. Status, diffs, branches, commits, merges and history. LouisAgent.Packs.DotNet The .NET SDK. Build, test, run and restore projects. LouisAgent.Packs.Shell Python, PowerShell and bash scripts. LouisAgent.Packs.Web The web. Search, read a page, check a quote, convert the money it names. LouisAgent.Packs.Docs A project's own docs. List, read and search its markdown. LouisAgent.Packs.Calculator Sums worked out in code, so a model doesn't do them in its head. LouisAgent.Packs.Leads Tells a site's owner that someone is interested. LouisAgent.Packs.Site Takes a visitor to a page of the site, and to a place on it. LouisAgent.Packs.Triage What a team triages a service's errors with, starting from the error feed. Build a pack Packs stay convertible to MCP The rules What every turn keeps. A few rules hold on every turn, whichever agent runs it. Each one is kept in code, not left to the prompt, so a model can't talk its way past it. arguments as data A tool gets its arguments as data, never pasted into a shell command, so model text can't become a new command. guard the context A tool result over 50,000 characters is summarised, a cut-off call is never run, and a failure says why it failed. history is append-only Nothing edits the system prompt, the tools or an earlier message. A finished turn is kept whole. measure every request Every request is priced in the ledger. A cost nobody knows is written as unknown, never as nought. take a site's no Every fetch obeys robots.txt and a page's no-AI signals, and says honestly what it is.
